title: Your Backup Plan Doesn't Mean You Failed
subtitle: A backup gives you options when Plan A doesn't work.

cards.title: 1 | Why backups help
cards.body: Plans change. Restaurants run out of things. Parties are unpredictable. A backup can keep one food problem from taking over the whole event.

cards.title: 2 | Backups can look different
cards.body: A backup might be a snack, food you brought, eating before an event, a second restaurant option, or knowing you can participate without eating.

cards.title: 3 | Backup ≠ failure
cards.body: Using your backup means the plan worked exactly as a backup is supposed to work.

content_body.source_evidence: Celiac Disease Foundation; Meyer & Naveh self-management framework

title: Planning Without Spending Forever Planning
subtitle: Good planning should help you live—not take over your life.

cards.title: 1 | Planning has a purpose
cards.body: Planning ahead can make daily activities easier and support decision-making, flexibility, and problem-solving.

cards.title: 2 | Use a minimum useful plan
cards.body: Ask: Where am I going? What food question actually matters? Who can help? What's my backup? You may not need to research every possible detail.

cards.title: 3 | Know when to stop
cards.body: Once you have enough information for your decision and a backup if needed, more searching may not add much. Your goal is to get back to the activity.

content_body.source_evidence: Meyer & Naveh (2021) self-management framework; teen-facing extension

title: How to Explain Celiac in 20 Seconds
subtitle: Clear beats complicated.

cards.title: 1 | Start with the essential point
cards.body: You can say: “I have celiac disease, so I need to eat gluten-free for medical reasons.”

cards.title: 2 | Add what matters for the situation
cards.body: At a restaurant you might add: “I also need to avoid cross-contact during preparation.” With a friend, you may only need the first sentence.

cards.title: 3 | You control the length
cards.body: You can give the 10-second version, explain more, or say you don't want to get into it. Self-advocacy does not require telling your whole medical story.

content_body.source_evidence: NIDDK factual basis + teen self-advocacy extension

title: Asking Without Apologizing
subtitle: A medical need is not a personal inconvenience you created.

cards.title: 1 | Notice the apology reflex
cards.body: It can be easy to start with “Sorry, but...” when asking about food. You can be courteous without apologizing for having celiac disease.

cards.title: 2 | Try neutral language
cards.body: Examples: “Could you tell me how this is prepared?” “I have celiac disease and need this to be gluten-free.” “Could we check one thing before I order?”

cards.title: 3 | Clear + kind works
cards.body: Being assertive does not mean being rude. Clear information can make it easier for other people to help.

content_body.source_evidence: Celiac Disease Foundation dining guidance + teen self-advocacy extension

title: It's Gluten-Free, But Do I Have Enough Information?
subtitle: “GF ingredients” and “enough information for me to decide” are different questions.

cards.title: 1 | Start with what you know
cards.body: Maybe the host says the ingredients are gluten-free. That's useful information.

cards.title: 2 | Ask what's still unknown
cards.body: Do you need to know how it was prepared? Whether utensils or serving areas were shared? Whether there is a package or another reliable source? The missing information depends on the situation.

cards.title: 3 | Make your decision
cards.body: You can ask more, choose a different option, use a backup, or decide not to eat. The app should help you identify information—not pressure you toward a particular food choice.

content_body.source_evidence: Beyond Celiac cross-contact guidance + teen lived-experience extension

title: When You've Asked the Questions and Still Feel Unsure
subtitle: Information and feelings can both be part of the moment.

cards.title: 1 | Check for a real information gap
cards.body: Is there a specific unanswered question about ingredients, preparation, or serving? If yes, you can ask it.

cards.title: 2 | Notice if the information question is finished
cards.body: Sometimes you have received the information you wanted and still feel nervous. Noticing that difference can help you understand what you're dealing with.

cards.title: 3 | You still own the choice
cards.body: You can choose another food, use a backup, not eat, or make the decision that feels appropriate to you. My C-Day should never make eating the “brave” answer.

content_body.source_evidence: Teen lived-experience synthesis; clinical/expert review required

title: When Food Feels Different After Diagnosis
subtitle: Your relationship with food can change, not just your grocery list.

cards.title: 1 | Food can carry new meaning
cards.body: A food you once loved may now look unappealing, feel risky, or remind you of something you cannot safely eat.

cards.title: 2 | Don't turn the reaction into a score
cards.body: You do not need to want gluten-containing food, and the app should not make “overcoming” disgust or worry into a challenge.

cards.title: 3 | Pay attention to your overall eating and well-being
cards.body: The goal is to have enough foods you can enjoy and to feel supported. If food-related fear or avoidance is significantly limiting eating or causing substantial distress, talk with a parent/caregiver and your celiac healthcare team.

content_body.source_evidence: Teen lived-experience synthesis; clinical review required

title: I Feel Like a Burden
subtitle: Needing consideration isn't the same as causing a problem.

cards.title: 1 | Why the feeling can show up
cards.body: Restaurant choices, parties, travel, and group food plans may sometimes change because you need a gluten-free option. That can create guilt even when nobody is blaming you.

cards.title: 2 | Look at what your friends are actually doing
cards.body: Friends who help choose a workable restaurant or ask what you need may be trying to include you—not telling you that you are difficult.

cards.title: 3 | You still have choices
cards.body: Sometimes you'll suggest a different place. Sometimes you'll eat beforehand. Sometimes you'll ask the group to help. There is no single correct social strategy.

content_body.source_evidence: Teen lived-experience synthesis; expert review required

title: Celiac Fatigue Is Different From Not Knowing What to Do
subtitle: You can know exactly what to do and still be tired of doing it.

cards.title: 1 | The work adds up
cards.body: Checking labels, researching restaurants, explaining celiac, planning backups, and thinking ahead can take mental energy.

cards.title: 2 | Skill doesn't erase effort
cards.body: Being experienced with celiac doesn't mean every decision becomes effortless. You can be good at self-management and still be tired of managing.

cards.title: 3 | Reduce the load when you can
cards.body: Use familiar options, repeat plans that work, ask other people to help, or choose a lower-effort strategy when appropriate.

title: From Speaking Up to Advocating
subtitle: Advocacy can be small, practical, and optional.

cards.title: 1 | Start with self-advocacy
cards.body: Self-advocacy is asking for the information, accommodations, or support you need.

cards.title: 2 | Advocacy can grow outward
cards.body: You might suggest that school event food information be shared earlier, help a friend understand cross-contact, correct a myth, or support someone newly diagnosed.

cards.title: 3 | You don't owe the world a lesson
cards.body: Having celiac does not make you responsible for educating everyone. Choosing not to advocate in a particular moment is also a valid choice.

content_body.source_evidence: Meyer & Naveh self-management framework + teen-facing advocacy extension
